entries.clue: Confusion with power in aid for late-night reading? (7)

blocks.note: bedlam is noisy confusion, the word left behind by the old London madhouse
P is the standard short form of power, as on a physics formula

annotation.surface: Confusion and electricity offered together as a help for reading after dark.
annotation.walkthrough: Bedlam takes its name from the Bethlem hospital in London, which is how a word for an asylum came to mean uproar. The question mark concedes that the definition describes the answer rather than naming it.
annotation.definitionFit: A bedlamp is the lamp on the bedside table, which is what gets switched on to read by once the rest of the house is asleep.

entries.clue: Show indignation getting cross amid Alice warring with Mike (7)

indicatorNotes.warring: Warring parties are set against one another rather than lined up in order, and letters at war will not stay as they were given.
indicatorNotes.amid: Amid means in among, so the letter it governs is dropped into the middle of the others rather than placed beside them.

blocks.note: the five letters of the name with Mike's M from the radio alphabet, shuffled and then opened after the first letter
a cross is written X, the mark made on a ballot paper

annotation.surface: Tempers rise in the middle of a quarrel between Alice and Mike.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Getting cross' reads as losing your temper and is one letter. Mike is M in the NATO radio alphabet, the same list that supplies Charlie, Oscar and Victor whenever a setter wants a single letter from a name.
annotation.definitionFit: To exclaim is to cry out suddenly, which is how indignation gets shown — the sharp word out loud rather than the silent sulk.

entries.clue: Restrict a lot of fruit with appeal (5)

indicatorNotes.a lot of: A lot of something is most of it and not the whole, so the word beside it arrives with its last letter missing.

blocks.note: the lime is the fruit, docked of its final letter
it is the old word for sex appeal, as in the It girl

annotation.surface: An instruction to cut down on most of the tempting fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It' for sex appeal comes from Elinor Glyn's 1927 novel and the silent-film It girl, and setters have kept it ever since. Both definition and answer are verbs, which rules out the noun sense of a boundary.
annotation.definitionFit: To limit something is to restrict it, setting a bound it may not pass, and the two verbs take the same sort of object.

entries.clue: Mother hiding a blemish has form of make-up (7)

indicatorNotes.hiding: To hide a thing is to keep it out of sight inside something else, so the letters it governs go within rather than alongside.

blocks.note: ma is the familiar word for mother, and the two letters split apart to take the rest
the article is taken at face value as one letter
a scar is the blemish left on skin once a wound has healed

annotation.surface: A mother covering up a mark on her face.
annotation.walkthrough: What the mother hides is both words, article included, which is easy to miss while the article still looks like grammar. 'Has' is holding the two halves of the clue together and doing nothing else.
annotation.definitionFit: Mascara is the make-up brushed onto eyelashes, so the definition names it by its class rather than by the job it does.

entries.clue: Sack put in French station for rubbish (7)

indicatorNotes.put in: What is put in a thing ends up inside it, so the first word's letters are set within the second's.

blocks.note: gare is the French for a railway station, as in the Gare du Nord
a sack is a bag, and the three letters go in whole

annotation.surface: A sack dumped at a station somewhere in France.
annotation.walkthrough: The French word is worth learning, since setters reach for it whenever a clue needs those four letters round something. 'Sack' hides its plainest meaning behind the dismissal-from-a-job sense the surface prefers.
annotation.definitionFit: Garbage is rubbish — household waste, and by extension the nonsense that gets talked — so the definition is a plain synonym.

entries.clue: Pilot has a struggle to keep a time (6)

indicatorNotes.to keep: To keep something is to hold on to it, and what is held is held inside.

blocks.note: an A and then VIE, since to vie with someone is to struggle against them
another A, then T, the standard short form of time

annotation.surface: A pilot fighting to keep to the timetable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pilot' is the verb here, to fly the aircraft, rather than the person in the seat. Each 'a' in the clue is doing duty as a letter of its own, which is what makes the six so hard to separate.
annotation.definitionFit: To aviate is to fly an aircraft, the verb behind aviation, and it matches 'pilot' used as a verb rather than a noun.

entries.clue: Sole cabin after renovation has projecting platforms (9)

indicatorNotes.after renovation: A renovation takes the place apart and puts it back in a different arrangement, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: A single cabin gaining platforms once the builders have finished.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sole' offers the fish and the underside of a shoe before settling into the adjective meaning only. Two words holding exactly nine letters between them is the signal to start shuffling.
annotation.definitionFit: Balconies are the platforms that jut out from the wall of a building, and the plural definition matches the plural answer.

entries.clue: Leave society facing cut and become very angry (2,5)

indicatorNotes.facing: To face something is to stand in front of it, so the single letter takes its place ahead of the word that follows.

blocks.note: to leave is to go
S is the usual short form of society in a club's own initials
to pare is to cut away at something, trimming or peeling it back

annotation.surface: Somebody walks out on a society facing cuts, thoroughly furious.
annotation.walkthrough: To go spare is British for losing your temper altogether, the phrase used of a parent who finds the car scratched. 'Cut' is the gardener's paring rather than the reduction in funding the surface wants.
annotation.definitionFit: To go spare is to become very angry indeed, a British idiom for flying off the handle, and both are verbs.

entries.clue: Engineer searched outer residence in a row (8,5)

indicatorNotes.Engineer: To engineer something is to contrive it into being, fitting the parts together to suit, and here the parts are letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

annotation.surface: An engineer going over the outermost house in a row.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like the subject of the sentence and is the instruction instead, which is why the shuffle is easy to miss. Terraced houses are the joined rows that fill British towns, each sharing its side walls with the next.
annotation.definitionFit: A terraced house is one of a row built joined together in a line, the standard British street terrace, so the definition describes its position as much as the building.

entries.clue: Dishonest scheme among shameless campers (4)

indicatorNotes.among: What is among a crowd sits inside it without being part of it, which is how these letters sit unbroken inside the words.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters bridging the gap between the two words

annotation.surface: Brazen campers running some kind of fiddle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shameless' is the sort of adjective that usually points at an anagram, and here it is present only to supply its last letter. Short hidden runs hide best when they straddle a space.
annotation.definitionFit: A scam is a fraud dressed up as a legitimate offer, which is a dishonest scheme in the plainest sense of both words.

entries.clue: I tip scales wrongly for expert (10)

indicatorNotes.wrongly: Done wrongly means not done as it should be, and letters put together wrongly are out of their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.surface: Somebody weighing things badly and throwing the balance out.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder begins at the clue's first word, so nothing stands in front of it to mark where the shuffle starts; counting to ten is what settles it. 'Expert' is the noun, the person rather than the quality.
annotation.definitionFit: A specialist is someone who has made a single field their own, so 'expert' is the noun naming exactly that person.

entries.clue: Fellow with skill recalled slogan (6)

indicatorNotes.recalled: To recall a thing is to call it back, and a word called back comes out in the opposite order.

blocks.note: a fellow is a man
skill is art, and those three letters are turned back to front

annotation.surface: A skilled fellow remembering the old catchphrase.
annotation.walkthrough: Art for skill is the older sense, the one in 'the art of conversation' rather than the one hanging in a gallery. A mantra is a phrase chanted in meditation, repeated until the words stop registering.
annotation.definitionFit: A mantra is a phrase said over and over, the meditator's chant and now the line a politician repeats, which is what a slogan is.

entries.clue: Reasonable allowance to introduce a learner (8)

indicatorNotes.to introduce: Whoever introduces the next act goes on first, so the allowance leads and the letters it brings on follow behind.

blocks.note: a ration is the fixed allowance handed out when something is scarce
the article stands as a single letter
L is the plate a British learner driver has to display

annotation.surface: A sensible allowance made so that a beginner can be brought in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reasonable' and 'allowance' sit side by side as though one described the other, and the split between definition and wordplay falls exactly between them. The L plate is red on white and compulsory until the test is passed.
annotation.definitionFit: Something rational is grounded in reason rather than feeling, which is the claim made by calling a decision reasonable; both are adjectives.

entries.clue: Name a club that’s arranged transport for patients (9)

indicatorNotes.arranged: To arrange things is to set them out in an order of your own choosing, not the order they arrived in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: Name the club that has laid on transport for the sick.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a request, which disguises the fact that its first three words are letters to be shuffled rather than an instruction to answer a question. 'That's' is joinery, holding the shuffle against what it produces.
annotation.definitionFit: An ambulance is the vehicle that carries the sick and injured to hospital, so the definition describes its whole job rather than naming its class.

entries.clue: Large chap in autumn shortly prepared final demand (9)

indicatorNotes.shortly: Shortly means cut short, so the season gives up its last letter before anything else is done with it.
indicatorNotes.prepared: Something prepared has been worked into shape rather than left as it was found, and these letters are worked into a new order.

blocks.note: L is the size on a clothing label
Tim is an everyday man's name standing in for any chap
the season with its final letter cut off

annotation.surface: A big fellow drawing up a last demand as autumn closes in.
annotation.walkthrough: A first name doing duty for 'chap' is standard setter's shorthand; the letters left over once the size and the season are counted out decide which name. Note the order — the season is docked first, and only then is everything shuffled.
annotation.definitionFit: An ultimatum is the last demand made before the talking stops and something worse follows, whether it comes from a government or a gas board.

entries.clue: Celebrity chef with no love for some offal (5)

indicatorNotes.with no: 'With no' announces an absence, so whatever is named after it comes out of the word before it.

blocks.note: Jamie Oliver is the British television cook, and the surname is what is wanted
love is nil in tennis scoring, written as the round letter

annotation.surface: A television cook who cannot abide offal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With no love for' reads as one phrase in the sentence and has to be broken up, since only the middle word names what is removed. Tennis is where a nought gets called love, from the shape of the figure.
annotation.definitionFit: Liver is the organ sold as offal — the edible innards a butcher keeps apart from the joints — so the definition names it by its family.

entries.clue: Idiots beginning to taunt comics (5)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: The beginning of a word is its first letter, and that is all the word beside it contributes.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
wits are the funny ones, people quick with a joke

annotation.surface: Fools starting to jeer at the comedians.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Comics' means the performers rather than the papers, and the plural noun for them is what the wordplay wants. Twit is mild British abuse, the exasperated schoolyard word rather than a real insult.
annotation.definitionFit: Twits are fools, and the plural definition matches the plural answer exactly.

entries.clue: Our lot, initially late to arrive, admitted willingly (7)

indicatorNotes.initially: What happens initially happens at the start, so only the opening letter of the word beside it is taken.

blocks.note: our lot, the speaker's own crowd, is we
the opening letter of the word
to arrive somewhere is to come

annotation.surface: Our crowd turned up late and were let in all the same.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'lot' makes the middle of the clue look like an aside about poor timekeeping, and that aside is a single letter. The definition is an adjective, the way a guest is described rather than an action taken.
annotation.definitionFit: A welcome visitor is one admitted willingly, gladly let in rather than merely tolerated, which is the adjective the definition spells out.

entries.clue: A daughter calling to get entry (9)

blocks.note: the article taken as the single letter it is
D is the short form of daughter used on family trees and in birth notices
a calling is a mission, the work somebody feels sent to do

annotation.surface: A daughter's vocation is what earns her a way in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Calling' looks like a participle — somebody shouting, or paying a call — and is the noun meaning a vocation. Three pieces in clue order with nothing rearranged makes this one of the gentler charades.
annotation.definitionFit: Admission is the being let in, entry to a building or a club, and both nouns name the act rather than the door.

entries.clue: This person’s urge to dazzle (7)

blocks.note: the setter's way of saying I, with the 's standing for is, so the two run together into a contraction
to press someone is to urge them, pushing for an answer

annotation.surface: The speaker's own desire to make a splash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This person' is how a setter refers to themselves in a clue, and the 's is the verb rather than a possessive — worth filing away, since it turns up constantly. 'Urge' here is the verb, not the noun the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: To impress someone is to dazzle them, leaving them admiring, and both are verbs taking a person as their object.

entries.clue: Former individual given money in game (3-4)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts the letter before it inside the word that follows rather than beside it.

blocks.note: an individual is a single one
a tie is a game in a knockout competition, the fixture two clubs are drawn to play
M is the crossword's letter for money

annotation.surface: Someone handed cash during a game.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen in the enumeration marks where the two pieces meet and is the best guide to the shape. 'Tie' for a game is football's word for a cup fixture, the match the draw pairs you with.
annotation.definitionFit: One-time means former — the one-time champion is the champion no longer — and it stands in front of a noun exactly as 'former' does.

entries.clue: Second little tyke quietly leaving is one with a deadly aim? (6)

indicatorNotes.leaving: What leaves a place is no longer in it, so the letter named just before goes out of the word it was in.

blocks.note: S is the clock's short form for second
a nipper is the British word for a small child
p is piano on a score, the composer's mark telling the player to drop the volume, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: A cheeky child slipping away without a sound.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition that describes rather than names. Tyke is northern English for a child, affectionate when it is not quite a complaint, and the deletion is signalled a word after the letter it removes.
annotation.definitionFit: A sniper is the marksman who picks off a target from cover, so the definition describes the job instead of naming the trade.

entries.clue: Fine language to describe a male wading bird (8)

indicatorNotes.to describe: To describe a circle is to draw all the way round it, so the language is drawn around the letters that follow.

blocks.note: F is the pencil grade marked fine, between HB and H
lingo is language, the jargon or the foreign tongue you cannot follow
the article stands as one letter
M is the tick-box short form of male

annotation.surface: Elegant words chosen to describe a man.
annotation.walkthrough: The wrapper opens after its own first letter, so only one letter of it stands ahead of what it takes in — the hardest part of the clue to see. 'Fine' is the pencil grade rather than the weather or the penalty.
annotation.definitionFit: A flamingo is the pink long-legged bird that feeds standing in shallow water, so the definition names the class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Steps to circle lake in locations (6)

indicatorNotes.to circle: To circle a thing is to go all the way round it, so the letter named lands inside the other word.

blocks.note: paces are steps, the ones counted out on the ground
L is the short form of lake used on maps

annotation.surface: Somebody stepping out a circle around a lake.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' is only joining the wordplay to the definition, though it reads like another part of the walk. Steps and paces agree in number, which is why the definition is plural too.
annotation.definitionFit: Places are locations, the spots on the map where things are, and both are plural nouns.

entries.clue: Stop in a university to make farewell (5)

indicatorNotes.in: In sets the word before it inside the letters that follow, rather than in front of them.

blocks.note: the article plus U, the usual short form of university, and the pair splits to take the other word
an engine that stops dies, and so does a conversation

annotation.surface: Breaking a journey at a university to say goodbye.
annotation.walkthrough: Adieu is the French for goodbye, borrowed into English for a parting meant to last. The container here is only two letters and is split between them, which is unusually thin cover for three.
annotation.definitionFit: Adieu is a farewell, the French goodbye kept in English for the more final sort of leave-taking.

entries.clue: Cleaner of some ivories? (10)

blocks.note: not the person who arrives with a mop, but the stuff that does the cleaning
on the surface the keys at the piano; the same slang names what a dentist inspects

annotation.surface: Somebody employed to polish the keys of a piano.
annotation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to take apart: the clue is a description, and 'ivories' carries it. The word is old slang for piano keys and equally old slang for teeth, false sets once having been carved from the real thing.
annotation.definitionFit: Toothpaste is the cleaner kept by the bathroom sink, and the ivories it cleans are teeth rather than the piano keys the surface points at.

entries.clue: Flower put in hair, I suppose (4)

indicatorNotes.put in: What is put in something sits inside it, and these letters sit inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters running from the middle of the first word and straight across the comma

annotation.surface: A bloom tucked into somebody's hair, apparently.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flower' in a cryptic is usually a river — a thing that flows — and this time it is the real thing. Punctuation is no barrier to a hidden run, and the comma counts for nothing at all.
annotation.definitionFit: The iris is the tall garden flower with sword-shaped leaves, and the singular definition matches the singular answer.

entries.clue: Study symbol in European country (7)

blocks.note: a den is the small room at home that gets worked in
a mark is a symbol set down on the page

annotation.surface: Some symbol noticed in a study somewhere in Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mark' was the German currency before the euro, which pulls the guess a country south of where it belongs. 'Study' is the room in the house rather than the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Denmark is the Scandinavian country between the North Sea and the Baltic, so the definition names it by its class.

entries.clue: Confident American for all to see in fancy dress (7)

indicatorNotes.fancy: Fancy dress is dress got up as something it is not, and letters got up that way are no longer in their own order.

blocks.note: A is the standard short form of American
U is the British film certificate, the rating meaning anyone at all may watch
anagram fodder, five letters

annotation.surface: A self-possessed American on open display at a costume party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dress' does two jobs: it completes the costume in the sentence and supplies five of the seven letters. The U certificate has meant universal, suitable for anybody, since the British censors started rating films.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone assured is confident, settled and unflustered in what they are doing, and both words are adjectives describing a person.
